# FDG4053

> AVOID publicly exposed nested types. The only exception to this guideline is if variables of the nested type need to be declared only in rare scenarios such as subclassing or other advanced customization scenarios.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 4.9 Nested Types.

## How it is checked

- Check: sdk (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: CA1034
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application none, test none
- Status: verified

Library only: the text is about publicly exposed nested types. CA1034 reports externally visible nested types; nested enums are not reported. The exception (types whose variables are declared only in rare scenarios such as subclassing, and the struct enumerators of the Cwalina and Barton annotations) cannot be detected; such reports are not violations. Moving a public nested type out of its enclosing type changes its full name, which changes the public API, so the fix is breaking; CA1034 has no code fix.

## From the book

> **Krzysztof Cwalina:** The main motivation for this guideline is that many beginner developers don’t understand why some type names have dots in them and some don’t. As long as they don’t have to type in the type name, they don’t care. But the moment you ask them to declare a variable of a nested type, they get lost. Therefore, in general, we avoid nested types and use them only in places where developers almost never have to declare variables of that type (e.g., collection enumerators).

> **Jeremy Barton:** The main scenario where we expose nested types in the Base Class Libraries is for struct-based enumerators (which also violate the guideline of not making mutable structs). We feel that these are generally OK because (a) they help with performance by avoiding heap-based allocation and interface dispatch and (b) they’re almost always used in a foreach statement and most callers aren’t aware that a struct enumerator was involved.
